0.value:
Stores what arrives in a tensor of fixed length, and either sends the whole store each time something arrives or hands back one stored position when asked.

It has three ways of filling and two ways of answering, which makes it two nodes in one. As a recorder of the recent past ("input is multi-channel sample" or "input is stream of samples" with "output buffer on every input") it keeps the last sample count arrivals and sends them oldest first - the demo at the top. As a store you read from (the default: "output samples on demand by index") it holds values and sends the one at the position you ask for - the demo at the bottom. For the recorder job alone, t.rolling_buffer is simpler and has a reset.

SYNTAX:
t.buffer <sample count> <dtype> <device>
Default sample count 256, float32, cpu.

EXAMPLE:
t.buffer 32

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

input:
Data to store. Every arrival is stored, and in "output buffer on every input" mode the buffer is then sent. A single number is one sample.

sample to output:
A position (an int, 0 = the first slot). The value stored there is sent - a single number, or a list for a multi-channel buffer. A position outside 0 to sample count - 1 is ignored. In the two stream modes this is a position in the store, not in time: the slots are written round and round, so slot 0 is not necessarily the oldest.

sample count (option):
How many samples are kept. At one sample per frame (60 a second) 60 is one second of history. A change takes effect at the next input: the buffer starts again, empty, at the new length.

update style (option):
"input is stream of samples" (the default) - each number that arrives is one sample, written into the next slot, wrapping round at the end. A list of several numbers writes them all in order, so a list exactly sample count long fills the store in one go.
"input is multi-channel sample" - each arrival (a list or 1-D tensor of N values) is ONE sample of N channels, stored as one row: the buffer is sample count rows by N columns. A single number is one sample of one channel. A different N starts a new, empty buffer. "buffer holds one sample of input" - each arrival simply replaces the whole buffer (a copy of it, whatever its length).

output style (option):
"output samples on demand by index" (the default) - nothing is sent when data arrives; send a position into "sample to output". "output buffer on every input" - after each arrival a copy of the whole buffer is sent, rotated so that the oldest sample is first and the newest last. Rows not yet filled are zeros, at the oldest end.

dtype / device / requires_grad (also inlets):
What the stored tensor is. Incoming data is converted to it. float32 (the default), float16, int64, uint8, bool, complex64 and complex128. The menu also lists the same types under their torch names (torch.float32, float, torch.float ...). There is no float64 here: a float64 NumPy array comes out float32.

OUTPUTS:

output:
The buffer (rows = samples, oldest first), or the value at one position.

READING THE DEMO:
Top: make_bump sends a bump 16 values wide that steps one place along every 60 ms. t.buffer 32, set to multi-channel and to output on every input, keeps the last 32 of them: the heat_map has one row per sample, oldest at the top, newest at the bottom, so the moving bump draws a diagonal stripe that scrolls up as new rows arrive. Change sample count in the node's options (16, or 64) and the store starts again at that length; the heat_map follows.
Bottom: a t.buffer 8 with the default settings. The message stores 8 numbers when the page opens (one list of 8 fills the 8 slots exactly). Drag the slider to read any slot back. Click the message after editing it to store new numbers.

RELATED:
t.rolling_buffer is the always-sends recorder with a reset. np.sequence and np.rolling_buffer do these jobs for NumPy arrays. capture~ records the audio graph.
